title: Reading for specific information
status: Owner approved v0.3.0 on 2026-10-27; teacher release to all eligible schools
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional draft, AI-assisted. The passages are original academic-style texts written for this lesson and describe general, widely reported ideas without citing specific studies. No third-party passages or assessment questions copied. Human editorial, factual, key, mapping, difficulty and originality review pending.
prerequisites: Lesson 2 (TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN evidence) and Lesson 5 (paraphrase recognition).
Teacher has checked actual Reading Screener states privately. Do not use screener passages or items in this lesson.
Each learner has a printed workbook. The passage is long enough that phone-only reading is not recommended.

objectives.text: Locate the paragraph that contains a specific type of information (a reason, an example, a caution, a justification) when a nearby paragraph shares its topic or key words.
Complete sentences whose wording paraphrases whole clauses of an academic passage, copying words accurately within a word limit and rejecting nearby distractors.
Match views to the groups who hold them when groups not in the list, and groups that respond to a view, are named close by.

levels.foundation: Paragraph topic labels written together after skimming; group names circled before Questions 10-15; teacher may name two possible paragraphs for a matching item, recorded as support.
levels.core: Complete Questions 1-9 independently in 10 minutes, then justify each answer with a quotation.
levels.extension: Questions 10-15 (matching features) independently in 6 minutes, then explain the trap in one wrong option.
levels.high_band: Complete all fifteen questions in 12 minutes with no support, then write the paraphrase pair (question words / passage words) for every answer.

blocks.title: Sixty-second scan
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; timed by the teacher
blocks.instructions: Find each answer in the notice as quickly as you can. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER.

stimulus.title: Campus library: summer arrangements
paragraphs: From 1 July the library will open at 10.00 instead of 8.30, and close at 18.00. The silent study floor will be closed for painting until 20 July; group rooms remain available but must be booked online. Printing is moved to the ground floor. Books borrowed in June may be kept until the start of term without renewal.

items.prompt: New opening time: ________
items.evidence: open at 10.00 instead of 8.30
items.reason: 8.30 is the old time.

items.prompt: Group rooms must be booked ________.
items.evidence: must be booked online
items.reason: The key word 'booked' appears just before the answer.

items.prompt: Which floor is closed for painting?
items.evidence: The silent study floor will be closed for painting
items.reason: The ground floor is mentioned for printing, not painting.

blocks.title: Cooling the city from the roof up
blocks.mode: Independent classroom practice after strategy modelling; not a Reading Screener
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-5: the passage has six paragraphs, A-F. Which paragraph contains the following information? Write the correct letter, A-F. NB You may use any letter more than once.

stimulus.title: Cooling the city from the roof up
paragraphs: On windless summer evenings, the core of a large metropolis may remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a disparity known as the urban heat island effect. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb solar radiation throughout the day and surrender it only gradually once the sun has set, while vehicles, air-conditioning units and industrial processes contribute heat of their own. Counter-intuitively, therefore, the contrast between town and country tends to peak not in the early afternoon, when sunlight is most intense, but several hours after dusk.

The consequences extend well beyond discomfort. Epidemiologists studying successive heatwaves have linked prolonged night-time warmth to a marked rise in emergency hospital admissions, arguing that bodies deprived of the chance to cool down overnight are less able to withstand the following day's heat; elderly residents of poorly ventilated top-floor apartments appear especially vulnerable. Electricity consumption climbs in parallel as air conditioners run for longer, and the waste heat these machines expel into the street intensifies the very problem they were bought to solve. For municipal authorities, lowering urban temperatures has consequently become as much a public health priority as an energy one.

Among the responses that have gained traction is the green roof, in which a layer of growing medium and vegetation is laid over a waterproof membrane. Plants dissipate heat through evapotranspiration: moisture drawn up through the roots evaporates from the leaves, carrying energy away with it. The substrate beneath them also functions as insulation, retarding the passage of heat into the rooms below. Thermal imaging of individual buildings has repeatedly shown planted roofs to be dramatically cooler on hot afternoons than adjacent bitumen surfaces, although readings taken on a single rooftop reveal little about conditions in the surrounding district.

The advantages, moreover, are unevenly distributed. Engineers note that a planted roof on a high-rise office block may keep its upper floors comfortable while doing almost nothing for the air at pavement level, where pedestrians actually experience the heat. Ecologists, for their part, caution that the thin mats of drought-tolerant sedum favoured by developers sustain only a fraction of the insect and bird life found in deeper, more varied plantings. Deeper substrate, however, is heavy when saturated, and a considerable proportion of older buildings could not bear the additional load without expensive structural reinforcement.

Expense is the objection that property owners raise most persistently. Installation typically costs substantially more than a conventional replacement roof, and irrigation during dry spells, weeding and the inspection of drainage outlets impose recurring costs thereafter. Owners contend, with some justification, that while the wider public enjoys cooler streets, the financial burden falls entirely on them. A number of municipalities have responded with subsidies or reduced stormwater fees, reasoning that vegetated roofs retain rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the sewers during heavy downpours.

Urban planners increasingly regard green roofs as one element of a broader strategy rather than a remedy in themselves. Street trees cast shade precisely where people walk, and reflective 'cool roofs', which bounce sunlight back rather than absorbing it, are far cheaper on buildings whose structure cannot support soil. Some planners also warn that grants concentrated on prestigious commercial developments risk cooling the districts that need it least. In their view, the question worth asking is not whether green roofs work in general but which combination of measures suits a particular neighbourhood's buildings, budget and residents.

items.prompt: an account of how conditions after dark may weaken people's capacity to cope with heat
items.evidence: bodies deprived of the chance to cool down overnight are less able to withstand the following day's heat
items.reason: 'Weaken people's capacity to cope' paraphrases 'less able to withstand'; 'after dark' paraphrases 'overnight'. Paragraph A is the trap: it mentions the hours after dusk, but only describes temperatures, not their effect on people.

items.prompt: an example of a way of coping with heat that makes the original problem worse
items.evidence: intensifies the very problem they were bought to solve
items.reason: Air conditioners are a way of coping; their waste heat 'intensifies' (makes worse) the problem. Paragraph A also lists air-conditioning units, but only as one source of heat, with no idea of a solution backfiring. B is used twice.

items.prompt: a caution against drawing wide conclusions from evidence collected at one location
items.evidence: readings taken on a single rooftop reveal little about conditions in the surrounding district
items.reason: 'One location' paraphrases 'a single rooftop'; 'wide conclusions' paraphrases 'conditions in the surrounding district'. Paragraph D is tempting because it also limits the benefits, but it gives reasons, not a warning about evidence.

items.prompt: a reference to the justification some local authorities give for offering financial help
items.evidence: reasoning that vegetated roofs retain rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the sewers
items.reason: 'Justification' paraphrases 'reasoning that'; 'financial help' covers subsidies and reduced fees. Paragraph F mentions grants, but it criticises where they go; it does not explain why authorities offer them.

items.prompt: mention of an option suited to buildings unable to carry a planted roof
items.evidence: are far cheaper on buildings whose structure cannot support soil
items.reason: The option is the cool roof. Paragraph D is the trap: it explains why older buildings cannot carry the load, but offers no alternative.

blocks.support: Foundation: after the two-minute skim, the class agrees a three-word topic label for each paragraph. The teacher may name two candidate paragraphs for one item; record which item.
blocks.extension: For Questions 3 and 5, explain why paragraph D is tempting but wrong in each case.
blocks.high_band: Write the question words and the passage words for each answer as paraphrase pairs.

blocks.title: Sentence completion
blocks.mode: Independent classroom practice; same passage as Questions 1-5
blocks.instructions: Questions 6-9: complete the sentences. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

stimulus.workbook_reference: Use the passage printed with Questions 1-5.

items.prompt: Contrary to what might be expected, a city is warmest compared with the countryside not when the sun is strongest but well after ________.
items.evidence: but several hours after dusk
items.reason: 'Contrary to what might be expected' paraphrases 'Counter-intuitively'. 'Early afternoon' is the trap: it is when sunlight is strongest, the time the sentence rules out.

items.prompt: Rooms directly under a green roof warm up less quickly because the growing layer provides ________.
items.evidence: The substrate beneath them also functions as insulation, retarding the passage of heat into the rooms below
items.reason: 'Warm up less quickly' paraphrases 'retarding the passage of heat'; 'growing layer' paraphrases 'substrate'. 'Evapotranspiration' cools the plants' surroundings, not the rooms below.

items.prompt: On a very tall building, a planted roof may leave temperatures at ________ largely unchanged.
items.evidence: doing almost nothing for the air at pavement level
items.reason: 'Leave largely unchanged' paraphrases 'doing almost nothing for'. 'Upper floors' is the trap: those are the parts the roof does cool.

items.prompt: Some councils charge owners of planted roofs lower ________ because these roofs hold back rainwater.
items.evidence: reduced stormwater fees
items.reason: 'Charge lower' paraphrases 'reduced'. 'Sewers' and 'drainage outlets' are nearby traps: neither is something an owner is charged.

blocks.support: Foundation: the teacher may name the paragraph for one item; record which item.
blocks.extension: Explain why 'sewers' and 'drainage outlets' are both wrong for Question 9.

blocks.title: Word match or meaning match?
blocks.instructions: For each pair, decide which choice is based on meaning and which only on a matching word or topic.

examples.label: Question 1, tempting choice: paragraph A, last sentence
examples.text: 'the contrast between town and country tends to peak ... several hours after dusk.'
examples.comment: Topic match only. It is about the night, but it describes temperatures, not what happens to people.

examples.label: Question 1, real match: paragraph B, sentence 2
examples.text: 'bodies deprived of the chance to cool down overnight are less able to withstand the following day's heat'
examples.comment: Meaning match. This explains how the night affects people's ability to cope.

examples.label: Question 4, tempting choice: paragraph F, sentence 3
examples.text: 'grants concentrated on prestigious commercial developments risk cooling the districts that need it least.'
examples.comment: Word match only. 'Grants' is financial help, but this criticises where the money goes; it gives no justification.

examples.label: Question 4, real match: paragraph E, last sentence
examples.text: 'reasoning that vegetated roofs retain rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the sewers'
examples.comment: Meaning match. 'Reasoning that' introduces the authorities' justification.

examples.label: Question 5, tempting choice: paragraph D, last sentence
examples.text: 'a considerable proportion of older buildings could not bear the additional load'
examples.comment: This names the problem buildings, but offers no option for them. The question asks for an option.

blocks.title: Who holds which view?
blocks.mode: Extension practice for all learners; foundation group guided by the teacher

stimulus.workbook_reference: Use the passage printed with Questions 1-5.

items.prompt: Public money may end up helping the places with the least need.
items.evidence: grants concentrated on prestigious commercial developments risk cooling the districts that need it least
items.reason: 'Public money' paraphrases 'grants'; 'places with the least need' paraphrases 'districts that need it least'. Property owners (B) also talk about money, but about who pays, not where grants go.

items.prompt: The most commonly installed vegetation contributes little to biodiversity.
items.evidence: the thin mats of drought-tolerant sedum favoured by developers sustain only a fraction of the insect and bird life
items.reason: 'Most commonly installed' paraphrases 'favoured by developers'; 'biodiversity' covers insect and bird life. Developers are named, but they choose the plants; the view belongs to ecologists.

items.prompt: Warmth that persists through the night undermines people's resilience the next day.
items.evidence: bodies deprived of the chance to cool down overnight are less able to withstand the following day's heat
items.reason: The epidemiologists argue this. 'Municipal authorities' appear in the same paragraph but hold a different view (about priorities).

items.prompt: Cooling achieved high above the ground may not reach the people who most feel the heat.
items.evidence: doing almost nothing for the air at pavement level, where pedestrians actually experience the heat
items.reason: 'High above the ground' paraphrases 'upper floors' of a high-rise. Planners (A) also mention where people walk, but about street trees.

items.prompt: Those who pay for green roofs are not the main beneficiaries.
items.evidence: while the wider public enjoys cooler streets, the financial burden falls entirely on them
items.reason: Owners pay; the public gains. Municipalities in the same paragraph respond to this view but do not hold it.

items.prompt: Choosing the right measures depends on the character of each local area.
items.evidence: which combination of measures suits a particular neighbourhood's buildings, budget and residents
items.reason: 'Each local area' paraphrases 'a particular neighbourhood'. A is used twice.

blocks.support: Foundation: the teacher asks learners to circle every group name in the passage first (including developers and municipal authorities, which are not in the list) and guides the first item; record support.
blocks.high_band: Paragraph D begins 'The advantages, moreover, are unevenly distributed.' Explain what this sentence contributes to the writer's argument and how it links paragraph C to paragraph D.

stages.title: Opening challenge: sixty-second scan
stages.student: Scan the notice for three answers in sixty seconds.
stages.teacher: Time sixty seconds aloud. Reveal after everyone has stopped writing. Ask how learners found each answer: number shape, key word, or meaning.
stages.say: You did not read every word. You looked for the kind of information you needed.
stages.check: Learners can say what they looked for in Q1 (a time).

stages.title: Strategy: what kind of information?
stages.student: Underline the information-type word in each of Questions 1-5 (account, example, caution, justification, option). Skim the passage for two minutes and write a three-word label beside each paragraph.
stages.teacher: Model one question: 'an example of a way of coping with heat that makes the original problem worse' needs a solution that backfires, not just the words 'air conditioning', which also appear in paragraph A. Run the two-minute skim. Foundation group agrees labels together; record this support.
stages.say: Matching information asks what a paragraph contains. The same topic often appears in two neighbouring paragraphs; only one contains the right kind of information. A letter can be used more than once.
stages.check: Every learner has six paragraph labels.

stages.title: Independent practice: Questions 1-9
stages.student: Core: answer Questions 1-9 alone in 10 minutes, then use the last 2 minutes to write a short quotation as evidence for each answer. High band: answer all fifteen questions in 12 minutes, no support.
stages.teacher: Time 10 minutes for the core group and 12 minutes for high-band learners, who work through Questions 10-15 without stopping. Keep answers private. Circulate and record any support given and to whom.
stages.say: Find the evidence first, then write the letter or words. Copy words exactly from the passage.
stages.check: Original answers committed before the review.

stages.title: Review Questions 1-5: word match or meaning match?
stages.student: Check answers. For any wrong answer, write whether you chose by word or by meaning. Keep your first answer visible.
stages.teacher: Reveal Q1-Q5 in groups, asking for learner evidence first. Then use the contrast slides for Q1, Q4 and Q5 to show topic-match and word-match traps.
stages.say: Paragraph F mentions grants, but the question asks for a justification. Which paragraph explains why authorities pay?
stages.check: Learners can explain why paragraph D is wrong for Q5.

stages.title: Review Questions 6-9: copy exactly, respect the limit
stages.student: Check spelling and word count. Mark any answer that changed the passage's words.
stages.teacher: Point out the nearby traps: 'early afternoon' for Q6, 'upper floors' for Q8, 'sewers' and 'drainage outlets' for Q9. A changed word form or misspelling would not be accepted in the test. Corrections remain guided practice.
stages.say: The question changes the passage's words; the answer does not. Find the meaning, then copy the passage's words exactly.
stages.check: Learners can explain the Q9 trap.

stages.title: Questions 10-15: who holds which view?
stages.student: Answer Questions 10-15 in 6 minutes. Groups not in the list (developers, municipal authorities) are traps. A letter can be used more than once.
stages.teacher: Time 6 minutes. Foundation group: circle every group name first and guide the first item; record support. High-band learners (already finished) write paraphrase pairs and answer the paragraph D purpose question.
stages.say: Find each group's name, read the whole sentence around it, and check the view really belongs to that group and not to someone near it.

stages.title: Review Questions 10-15
stages.student: Check answers and quote the evidence. Mark any answer where you chose a group only because its name was nearby.
stages.teacher: Reveal answers. Highlight Q11 (developers named, ecologists hold the view) and Q14 (municipalities respond, owners hold the view). Ask a high-band learner to explain the function of 'The advantages, moreover, are unevenly distributed' (it turns from how green roofs work to their limits).
stages.say: Matching features tests who says what, just like matching speakers in Listening.
stages.check: Learners can name the trap in Q11 and Q14.

stages.title: My reading log
stages.student: In the reading log at the end of the workbook, record each wrong answer, the trap type (word match, word limit, wrong group) and one strategy for next time.
stages.teacher: Circulate and note trap types learners actually record. Do not convert this score to a band.
stages.say: Your log shows which strategy to practise. One task is not your reading level.
stages.check: Each learner has one strategy target.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and take the homework sheet.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets. Assign online practice only through the existing reviewed workflow. Record the date for the withheld fresh check.
stages.say: Next lesson you will build arguments for Writing Task 2. The reading skill you used today, finding exact support, will help you there too.
stages.check: Everyone knows the homework and next check date.

blocks.title: Saving seeds for the future
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-3: which paragraph, A-E, contains the following information? Questions 4-6: complete the sentences with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.

stimulus.title: Saving seeds for the future
paragraphs: Around the world, more than a thousand seed banks store the seeds of crops and wild plants. Their purpose is simple to state: if a variety disappears from farms or from the wild, stored seeds can be used to grow it again. Some collections are small and serve a single region; others hold samples from almost every country.

Seeds survive longest when they are dry and cold. Before storage, they are dried until they contain very little moisture, then sealed in airtight packets and kept at around minus twenty degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many species can remain alive for decades, and some for far longer.

Not every plant cooperates. The seeds of oaks, avocados and many tropical trees are killed by drying, so they cannot be stored in the usual way. For these species, banks are experimenting with freezing small pieces of the seed's embryo in liquid nitrogen, a technique that is expensive and requires specialist staff.

Storage alone is not enough. Staff must test samples regularly by germinating a few seeds, because a collection that appears healthy may have quietly lost its ability to sprout. When germination rates fall, the remaining seeds must be planted and new seed harvested, a process called regeneration.

Some scientists argue that seed banks should complement rather than replace conservation in the field. A variety stored in a freezer stops evolving, while one grown by farmers continues to adapt to changing pests and climate. For this reason, several banks now work directly with farming communities, returning seeds to the regions they came from.

items.prompt: a reason why some species need a different storage method
items.evidence: are killed by drying, so they cannot be stored in the usual way
items.reason: Drying kills these seeds, so normal storage fails.

items.prompt: an explanation of why stored seeds must be checked
items.evidence: may have quietly lost its ability to sprout
items.reason: Testing is needed because seeds can die without visible signs.

items.prompt: a benefit of growing crops on farms rather than only storing them
items.evidence: continues to adapt to changing pests and climate
items.reason: Field-grown varieties keep adapting; stored ones stop evolving.

items.prompt: Before storage, dried seeds are sealed in ________ packets.
items.evidence: sealed in airtight packets
items.reason: Copy the word exactly.

items.prompt: Pieces of some embryos are frozen in ________.
items.evidence: freezing small pieces of the seed's embryo in liquid nitrogen
items.reason: Two words, within the limit.

items.prompt: Planting old seeds to produce new seed is called ________.
items.evidence: a process called regeneration
items.reason: 'Is called' paraphrases 'a process called'.
